frameworks.name: Management Diamond
frameworks.definition: A framework identifying four reasons why people don't execute: they don't know they need to do it, they don't know how to do it, they don't know when to do it, or something is blocking them; the fourth category is motivation.

frameworks.name: Activity Rank-Ordering via Time Study
frameworks.definition: A time-tracking system where the founder logs activities every 15 minutes over one week, then ranks them by revenue impact to identify which tasks are highest-leverage and unique vs. delegatable.

claims.text: Key-man risk is the number one risk in every scaling service business for two reasons: first, no one wants to buy a founder-dependent business; second, the founder eventually burns out from overcommitment and wants to kill the business themselves.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Service-based business model
Founder personally involved in delivery or key relationships
claims.mechanism: When a single founder manages all client relationships and high-value delivery, the business becomes unsellable and the founder faces inevitable burnout, making exit or delegation impossible.

claims.text: In premium service businesses, technicians can generate $180,000 to $300,000 in annual revenue each, making technician acquisition a critical capital allocation problem rather than a recruiting problem.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Premium service business (high client willingness-to-pay)
Technician-dependent delivery model

claims.text: When a business owner cannot or will not delegate, the true constraint is not external (market, resources) but internal choice: the stated inability to recruit more technicians masks the unwillingness to relinquish control.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Founder expresses recruitment difficulty
Founder has adequate margins to fund hiring
claims.mechanism: Perceived constraints (need for founder involvement in every aspect) block growth more effectively than actual resource limits. The business owner frames inability as unwillingness by claiming to "have to" be involved when the real barrier is ego/control.
bounded_by: Applies when margins are sufficient to fund quality hires
Does not apply when founder is truly the only person capable of the core work (e.g., sole practitioner professional)

claims.text: Founder activities should be rank-ordered by revenue impact via a systematic time study: the bottom half of the activity list (lowest revenue, most delegatable) should be identified and assigned to existing staff with bandwidth or new hires.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Service business with founder doing multiple roles
Business has premium margins to fund additional hires
claims.mechanism: Ranking founder activities by revenue impact reveals which tasks are highest-leverage and unique (founder should keep) vs. low-leverage and delegatable (should be reassigned). This breaks the founder's emotional resistance to delegation by making the decision data-driven rather than feeling-based.

claims.text: If a founder could recover 50% of their time through delegation, they could double the revenue of a service business while maintaining or improving margins.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Service business with founder bottleneck
Founder is not the core technical delivery resource
Business has premium client relationships and pricing
claims.mechanism: Founder time spent on non-core activities (admin, client management, low-leverage delivery) is forgone revenue. Redistributing this time to a new hire who can handle half the founder's responsibilities unlocks proportional revenue growth without new capital or market expansion.
bounded_by: Does not apply to businesses where founder is the irreplaceable technical expert (e.g., specialized medical practice)
Assumes existing demand can absorb doubled output

claims.text: Premium service businesses serving affluent clients should target premium technicians and be willing to spend significant acquisition costs (e.g., $50,000 signing bonuses with relocation packages) to recruit talent, because premium pricing creates excess margins that justify high hiring investment.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Premium service business ($300k+ per technician revenue)
Serving high-net-worth or institutional clients
Gross margin >50%
claims.mechanism: Premium clients pay premium prices, creating high margins. These margins should be reinvested in premium hiring (higher salaries, relocation bonuses) rather than cost-cutting on talent. High-quality technicians are a capital allocation problem: spend $50k to acquire a tech who generates $180-300k in revenue = positive ROI.
bounded_by: Does not apply to businesses serving price-sensitive or low-margin markets
Assumes the business has excess cash or margin to fund upfront hiring costs

claims.text: National recruitment ads combined with generous relocation packages (structured as signing bonuses, split into installments like $25k upfront and $25k at six months) unlock technician pipeline scaling for premium service businesses.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Premium service business recruiting specialized technicians
Sufficient margins to fund relocation packages
Local labor market is supply-constrained
claims.mechanism: Geographic constraint (must find local talent in a specific city) is a self-imposed limit. Running national ads taps a national labor pool; relocation bonuses remove the friction of geographic relocation. Splitting the bonus (50% upfront, 50% at six months) reduces immediate cash burn while ensuring retention through a six-month cliff.

claims.text: The founder's ego-driven insistence on involvement in every aspect of the business ('I have to be involved in every single aspect') is a major driver of key-man risk and prevents delegation, even when the business could handle more revenue if those tasks were redistributed.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Founder is profitable and has capacity to grow
Founder claims ownership/control of premium client relationships
claims.mechanism: Ego and status from being "the guy" clients want creates psychological resistance to delegation. The founder frames this as necessity ('I have to'), but it is actually preference ('I choose to'). This framing shields the ego from confrontation and allows the founder to avoid the growth conversation.

claims.text: When a service business has premium clients and high margins, mediocrity on the team is intolerable and should be replaced with premium talent, even if the cost is high relative to current payroll.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Premium service business with affluent client base
High gross margin (>50%)
Founder wants to scale revenue
claims.mechanism: Premium pricing attracts premium clients who expect premium delivery. Low-quality team members on a premium team degrade the brand promise and create client friction. Premium clients are worth premium team investment; the margin spread justifies higher salaries and selection standards.
bounded_by: Does not apply to price-sensitive markets or low-margin businesses
Assumes client experience is sensitive to team quality (true for high-touch service, less true for transactional service)

claims.text: When someone asks the question 'What stops you from recruiting?' and they admit they have no active recruiting process ('I kind of just gave up lately'), the issue is not market unavailability of talent—it is lack of intentional, resourced recruiting effort.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business has margin and profitability
Business owner has not run recruiting process recently
claims.mechanism: Talent acquisition is a process that requires active investment (ads, recruiter fees, relocation packages, screening calls). Passivity is indistinguishable from unavailability—if you're not recruiting, you won't find talent. The owner's surrender ('gave up') masks the unwillingness to invest in hiring.

examples.text: A technician service business in Bozeman, Montana serving high-net-worth clients at the Yellowstone Club (including notable affluent clients) operates with just five people (the owner, four technicians, and his wife handling admin). The owner generates $1.5M revenue year-to-date with ~$700k net profit. Despite having excess margins and the capacity to double revenue with more technicians, the owner hasn't actively recruited because he is unwilling to delegate client relationships he views as dependent on his personal involvement—even though these relationships are actually the highest-leverage activity he could protect. When pressed on what would stop him from recruiting, he admits the real blocker is ego: 'It's hard to let that go, you know, that ego.'

A service business owner claims to serve premium clients at a premium price point but hasn't conducted a systematic time study of their own activities. If they did, they would likely discover that relationship management (the highest-leverage activity) comprises only 20-30% of their time, while the remaining 70% goes to delivery, admin, and other low-leverage work that could be delegated to existing staff or new hires. Once this distribution is visible, the founder can reassign the bottom 50% of activities, freeing up 30-40% of their time, which directly translates to 50-100% revenue growth if the market can absorb it.

practices.text: Conduct a one-week time study: set an alarm every 15 minutes and log what you did in the last 15 minutes. At the end of the week, rank all activities by revenue impact and identify which are highest-leverage (keep for yourself) and which are delegatable (assign to existing staff or hire for).

To recruit premium technicians in a supply-constrained geographic market, run national recruitment ads and offer a generous relocation package structured as a signing bonus split into two installments (e.g., $25k upfront, $25k at six months) to reduce early churn.

Keep hiring as W-2 employees, not 1099 contractors. If someone works on your schedule, in your location, and per your specifications, they are employees under law and should be treated as such for compliance and legitimacy.

Use the Management Diamond framework to diagnose why team members or business functions aren't executing: they don't know they need to do it, they don't know how to do it, they don't know when to do it, something is blocking them, or there's a motivation issue. Address the right lever for each diagnosis.

As a founder, distinguish between activities you 'have to' do (true constraints) and activities you 'choose to' do (ego, control, or preference). If you choose to do something, that is a constraint you have imposed, not one imposed on you.
